hints: Count every carbon in the ring plus the side chain, then count all hydrogens from the OH groups and CH units to get the molecular formula first.
walkthrough:
Count atoms to get the molecular formula**
Look closely at Fig. 4.1. The side chain has 2 carbons and the lactone ring has 4 carbons, so 6 carbons in total. Counting hydrogens gives 8 and oxygens gives 6, so the molecular formula is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6$.

Simplify to the empirical formula**
Empirical means the simplest whole number ratio. All of 6, 8 and 6 divide by 2, so divide through to get $\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_3$.

hints: Recall that $n = c \times V$ needs volume in $\text{dm}^3$, so think how to convert $28.40 \text{ cm}^3$ before multiplying by $5.00 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough:
Set up the moles calculation**
For any solution, amount is concentration times volume: $$n(\text{I}_2) = c \times V$$ Concentration is already in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, so volume must be in $\text{dm}^3$.

Convert and substitute**
$$V = \frac{28.40}{1000} = 0.02840 \text{ dm}^3$$ $$n = 5.00 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.02840 = 1.42 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}$$
Final answer: amount of $\text{I}_2 = 1.42 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}$

hints: Use the equation in Fig. 4.2 to link moles of $\text{I}_2$ from (b)(i) to moles of vitamin C in the $5.00 \text{ cm}^3$ sample.
Think how to go from the mass in the small $5.00 \text{ cm}^3$ portion to the mass in the whole $200.0 \text{ cm}^3$ flask using $M_r = 176$.
walkthrough:
Link moles of iodine to moles of vitamin C**
Fig. 4.2 shows $1$ mol of $\text{I}_2$ reacts with $1$ mol of vitamin C. So the $5.00 \text{ cm}^3$ sample also contains $1.42 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}$ of vitamin C.

Find the mass in the titrated sample**
Mass is moles times $M_r$: $$m = 1.42 \times 10^{-5} \times 176 = 2.499 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g}$$ This is only the vitamin C in the $5.00 \text{ cm}^3$ pipetted portion.

Scale up to the whole tablet**
The tablet was made up to $200.0 \text{ cm}^3$, which is $200/5 = 40$ times larger: $$m(\text{tablet}) = 2.499 \times 10^{-3} \times 40 = 0.099968 \text{ g} \approx 0.100 \text{ g}$$

Final answer: mass of vitamin C in $5.00 \text{ cm}^3 = 1.42 \times 10^{-5} \times 176 = 2.50 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g}$
mass in tablet $= 2.50 \times 10^{-3} \times 200/5 = 0.100 \text{ g}$

hints: Compare $\text{I}_2$ with $2\text{I}^-$ in Fig. 4.2 and think which species gains electrons while vitamin C loses hydrogen.
walkthrough:
Spot who is oxidised and who is reduced**
Vitamin C loses two hydrogens to form Q with two new $\text{C=O}$ groups. Loss of hydrogen is oxidation. At the same time $\text{I}_2$ becomes $2\text{I}^-$, which is gain of electrons, so reduction.

Name the role**
A reagent that oxidises another species while itself being reduced is an oxidising agent. So $\text{I}_2$ acts as the oxidising agent here.
Final answer: oxidising agent, as $\text{I}_2$ is reduced to $\text{I}^-$ while vitamin C is oxidised to Q

hints: Look at the side chain of vitamin C and Q in Fig. 4.2 and notice the primary and secondary alcohol groups that stay unchanged with $\text{I}_2$.
Look at the $\text{C=C}$ inside the ring that remains as part of the product Q, and recall what hot concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$ does to alkenes.
walkthrough:
See why iodine is gentle and selective**
$\text{I}_2$ is a mild oxidising agent. It only removes hydrogen from the two enol OH groups to give the two ketone $\text{C=O}$ groups in Q. Everything else is left alone.

Predict attack on the alcohol side chain**
Hot concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ is very powerful. It would not stop there. It would also oxidise the $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ primary alcohol and the $\text{CH(OH)}$ secondary alcohol in the side chain, for example to carboxylic acids and ketones.

Predict attack on the alkene**
The ring contains a $\text{C=C}$ bond. Mild $\text{I}_2$ leaves the carbon skeleton intact, but hot concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$ breaks both the sigma and the pi bond of $\text{C=C}$, cleaving the molecule instead of giving clean Q.

Final answer: 1. Hot concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ would also oxidise the primary and secondary alcohol groups in the side chain.
2. It would also break both the sigma and pi bond of the $\text{C=C}$ bond, cleaving the ring.

hints: Compare the structures of vitamin C and Q in Fig. 4.3 and list the bonds that appear in both, ignoring the enol OH and $\text{C=C}$ that are lost.
Use Table 4.1 to match each retained bond to its wavenumber range and the specific group, such as ester or hydroxy, that contains it.
walkthrough:
Focus only on what is unchanged**
You need absorptions seen in both spectra, so ignore changes. Both molecules keep the lactone ester ring and both keep the $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH(OH)}$ side chain alcohols. Those shared bonds will give shared peaks.

Pick two shared bonds with data**
A good pair is the ester $\text{C=O}$ at $1710-1750 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ from the lactone carbonyl, and the hydroxy $\text{O-H}$ at $3200-3650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ from the side chain alcohols. Both appear in vitamin C and in Q.

Present bond, group and wavenumber together**
For each mark you must give all three linked: wavenumber range, bond, and specific functional group. For example: $1710-1750 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, $\text{C=O}$, ester. And: $3200-3650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, $\text{O-H}$, hydroxy alcohol.

Final answer: $\text{C=O}$ ester at $1710-1750 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to ester carbonyl present in both;
$\text{O-H}$ hydroxy at $3200-3650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to alcohol OH groups in side chain present in both (ALLOW: $\text{C-O}$ at $1040-1300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ for ester/hydroxy, $\text{C-H}$ at $2850-2950 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ for alkane).
